Claws, boutons, calyx geometry and the outside-ROI version

QuestionHow are PN boutons and KC claws found from synapse positions, how are APL synapses placed on them, how is the calyx drawn, and which synapses does the second version of the tables add?
Inputs
  • Raw PN → KC synapses in the calyx of each connectome (positions of T-bars and PSDs)
  • The APL synapse tables of Report 01
Outputs
  • <dataset>_PN_boutons_derived.csv.gz, <dataset>_KC_claws_derived.csv.gz
  • columns claw_id, nearest_claw_id, claw_dist_nm, bouton_id, nearest_bouton_id, bouton_dist_nm of the APL tables
  • with_outside_ROI_synapses/ (the second version of every table and plot)
  • odor_weighted/calyx_shape_by_dataset.csv/.png
Scripts

  • scripts/run.py (claws, boutons, assignment)
  • scripts/offroi/assign.py (synapses outside the official ROIs)

  • scripts/reports/r02_prep.py (claw purity and the example cells for this report)
  • scripts/reports/r02_claws_boutons.py (this report)

None of the four connectomes publishes which synapses form a PN bouton or a KC claw, so both are derived here from synapse positions. They matter because odor information enters the calyx bouton by bouton: each bouton belongs to one PN and so to one glomerulus, and each claw takes most of its input from one bouton. Reports 03, 04, 05 and 10 use claws and boutons to give APL synapses a glomerulus.

1Clustering sites into boutons and claws

Both units are found with the same rule, single-linkage clustering at dlink=2d_{\mathrm{link}} = 2dlink​=2 µm, applied to one neuron at a time:

  • Boutons. Take every T-bar of one antennal-lobe PN that has a KC or other partner in the calyx (one point per T-bar, however many PSDs it faces). Link any two T-bars closer than 2 µm. Each connected group is one bouton.
  • Claws. Take every PSD on one KC that faces a PN T-bar in the calyx. Link any two closer than 2 µm. Each connected group is one claw.
s∼s′  ⟺  ∃ s=s0,s1,…,sm=s′ (sites of one neuron): ∥xsl−xsl−1∥<dlink  ∀ l(1)s \sim s' \iff \exists\ s=s_0, s_1, \dots, s_m=s' \text{ (sites of one neuron)}:\ \lVert \mathbf{x}_{s_{l}} - \mathbf{x}_{s_{l-1}} \rVert < d_{\mathrm{link}}\ \ \forall\, l \tag{1}s∼s′⟺∃ s=s0​,s1​,…,sm​=s′ (sites of one neuron): ∥xsl​​−xsl−1​​∥<dlink​  ∀l(1)
Two sites are in the same unit when they are linked by such a chain; a unit can therefore be longer than 2 µm.

Units are numbered by size within each neuron (_bouton1 and _claw1 are the largest). For each claw the table also stores its number of PN synapses, its main PN π(c)\pi(c)π(c) (the PN with most synapses on it), that PN's type, its main bouton (the bouton holding most of those T-bars) and its centroid. Each claw then has a glomerulus: that of its main PN. Figure 1 shows one PN and one KC.

1.1How many, and how pure

smain(c)  =  #{s∈claw(c):s faces a T-bar of π(c)}∣claw(c)∣(2)s_{\mathrm{main}}(c) \;=\; \frac{\#\{s \in \mathrm{claw}(c) : s \text{ faces a T-bar of } \pi(c)\}}{|\mathrm{claw}(c)|} \tag{2}smain​(c)=∣claw(c)∣#{s∈claw(c):s faces a T-bar of π(c)}​(2)

Hemibrain KCs have 8 claws (median) and male CNS KCs 7; FlyWire 7, BANC 5. Published counts from light microscopy and EM are about 5–7 claws per KC; a 2 µm linking distance can split a large claw in two, so these counts are a little high. Claws are pure: 94% (hemibrain) and 95% (male CNS) of claws get at least 90% of their PN synapses from one PN, so naming a claw by its main PN's glomerulus loses little.

2Placing APL synapses on claws and boutons

For each APL synapse eee with a KC in the calyx, take the KC-side site (the PSD when APL is presynaptic, the T-bar when the KC is), and find the nearest PN → KC PSD of that same KC. Its distance is δ(e)\delta(e)δ(e) (column claw_dist_nm), and its claw is nearest_claw_id. The synapse is on a claw (claw_id filled) when δ(e)≤dassign=2\delta(e) \le d_{\mathrm{assign}} = 2δ(e)≤dassign​=2 µm. APL synapses with PNs are placed on boutons the same way, with the PN-side site and the T-bars of that PN.

δ(e)=min⁡s ∈ PSDs of PN input on KC(e)∥xeKC−xs∥,e is on claw claw(arg⁡min⁡s)  ⟺  δ(e)≤2 μm(3)\delta(e) = \min_{s \,\in\, \mathrm{PSDs\ of\ PN\ input\ on\ KC}(e)} \lVert \mathbf{x}_{e}^{\mathrm{KC}} - \mathbf{x}_s \rVert,\qquad e \text{ is on claw } \mathrm{claw}\big(\arg\min_s\big) \iff \delta(e) \le 2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \tag{3}δ(e)=s∈PSDs of PN input on KC(e)min​∥xeKC​−xs​∥,e is on claw claw(argsmin​)⟺δ(e)≤2 μm(3)

Almost every APL ↔ PN synapse in the calyx sits on a bouton, as expected: APL contacts the boutons. Only a minority of KC ↔ APL synapses sit on a claw, more so for APL → KC than for KC → APL: in the calyx most KC ↔ APL synapses are on the KC dendrite between claws, or on its fine branches. The column claw_dist_nm lets anyone re-cut at another distance.

Where this is used

Report 03 colors KC ↔ APL synapses by the odor response of their claw's glomerulus, using only synapses on a claw.

Report 04 counts APL → KC synapses on the claws of each glomerulus (the claw weight qgq_gqg​).

Report 10 measures distances along APL between the APL sites of the claws and boutons of different glomeruli.

3Drawing the calyx: the posterior view

Every map in these reports shows the calyx as seen from behind the fly (posterior view), with the fly's right to the right and dorsal up, so that all datasets look alike. Each dataset has its own axes, so the view is built from its native coordinates (Table 2), checked against mushroom-body landmarks (the lobes are anterior and ventral of the calyx, the vertical lobe is dorsal).

Table 2. Native axes used for the posterior view. Coordinates are in nm in the tables and µm in the maps.
DatasetRight (x of the map)Dorsal (y of the map)Anterior–posterior (depth)Note
FlyWire 783xxx−y-y−yzzzFlyWire coordinates are mirror-imaged relative to its side labels, so sides come from the labels
Hemibrain v1.2−x-x−x−z-z−zyyythe hemibrain yyy axis is anterior–posterior
Male CNS v1.0−x-x−x−y-y−yzzz
BANC 888−x-x−xzzzyyy

The calyx outlines still differ between datasets in these maps, mainly because each brain sits at a slightly different angle. The calyx is a flattened cup; its thinnest axis is tilted from the anterior–posterior axis by 25° (Hemibrain v1.2 R), 18° (Male CNS v1.0 L), 25° (Male CNS v1.0 R), and by 35–41° in BANC, so BANC's calyx is seen more obliquely and looks flatter. odor_weighted/calyx_shape_by_dataset.png shows every calyx from three sides.

4The second version: synapses just outside the official ROIs

Each connectome defines its mushroom body regions with its own ROI meshes. These meshes do not always cover the whole structure. In the male CNS the calyx ROIs leave out the posterior part of each calyx; in FlyWire and BANC the meshes of nearby neuropils (CRE, SIP, SMP) take in parts of the lobes. Yang decided (2026-10-14) to keep both versions: the official-ROI tables stay as they are, and with_outside_ROI_synapses/ holds the same tables, plots and maps with these synapses added back. The rule, in order:

  1. Anchors. Calyx: the PN → KC synapses inside the official calyx ROI, extended through PN → KC synapses outside every MB ROI that connect to them in steps of ≤ 3 µm (claws the ROI cut off). Peduncle and lobes: the APL ↔ KC synapses inside the official peduncle and lobe ROIs.
  2. Growing through KC synapses. APL ↔ KC synapses outside every MB ROI join the first anchor that reaches them in steps of ≤ 3 µm, and take that anchor's region. KC dendrites and axons exist only in the mushroom body, so these chains stay inside it.
  3. Joining. Any other synapse outside every MB ROI joins when its postsynaptic site lies within 3 µm of an anchor point, with the region of the nearest one (the calyx wins ties).
  4. Accessory calyces stay out. No chain runs through synapses with γd or αβp KCs, whose dendrites form the accessory calyces.
  5. PN synapses next to the calyx join only if they are PN → KC or their T-bar belongs to a calyx bouton.

Every added row is flagged in mb_region_source; keeping the rows marked official ROI gives the main tables back exactly (checked when the second version was built).

Table 3. Synapses added in the second version. Added synapses as a count and as a share of the official-ROI count, from with_outside_ROI_synapses/added_synapses_summary.csv. The male CNS calyx gains the most (+31% of APL synapses).

With the added synapses, male CNS PN input per KC matches hemibrain (96 synapses per KC in both), and its calyx KC ↔ APL synapses per KC go from 38% below hemibrain's to 20% below. Every analysis from Report 03 on is done in both versions.

Caveats

Where an accessory calyx touches the calyx or peduncle, some synapses with γd and αβp KCs within 3 µm of an anchor still join (male CNS 1,291; hemibrain 1,487). They are flagged rows with partner_type KCg-d or KCab-p.

The 3 µm steps are a choice. They were checked by eye on maps of the added synapses (with_outside_ROI_synapses/where_synapses_were_added.png), not against a ground truth.
